meta.title: Bulgarian A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bulgarian → English (see the Bulgarian, recall the meaning) and English → Bulgarian (see an English meaning, recall the Bulgarian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Bulgarian word list is published that a deck could take whole, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 337 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs and study, clothes, more food and cooking, the rooms and furniture of a home, the town and its services, travel and holidays, nature, the seasons and the compass, animals, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, sport and holidays, telling what happened when, the higher numbers and measures, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing, cooking and doing — and the other 413 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bulgarian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic with its stress marked (кни́га, чета́), because Bulgarian stress can fall on any syllable and move as the word changes (град, градове́), and nothing else shows it; there is no transliteration, and the Bulgarian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters. A verb is given in its first person singular present, the form a Bulgarian dictionary lists (чета́ 'I read', glossed 'to read'), since Bulgarian has no infinitive. The 360 nouns show their gender, their definite form (Bulgarian puts 'the' on the end of the word: кни́гата), their plural and, where it differs, the form used after a number; the 207 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, with the other verb of the pair beside them, their ти form and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's forms and every verb's present, past tenses and imperative by person, with the personal pronouns' full and short forms. Real example sentences come with 694 of the 750 words, three apiece for 598 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, stress and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

Тази илюзия е своеобразен затвор за нас, ограничавайки ни в рамките на нашите лични желания и привързаността към най-близките ни хора. A human being is part of the whole, called by us Universe, a part limited in time and space.
